newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Ashton denies CSO rift hit profit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Ashton denies CSO rift hit profit.

text.p: Australian diamond miner Ashton Ltd has blamed Russian selling, not its recent exit from the world diamond cartel, for lower profits expected in calendar 1997.

Commenting on Ashton's warning of leaner profits this year, managing director John Robinson said a slump in sales revenue after the company's mid-1996 divorce from the Central Selling Organisation (CSO) mainly reflected a weakening world market.
"At this stage, there's no reason for us to believe that we would be any different in terms of our pricing and sales position than if we had been selling through the CSO," he said.

On Monday, Ashton said in response to a share-price query from the Australian Stock Exchange that it expected its results for the six months ending June 30 to reflect the previous half-year, rather than the corresponding period a year ago.
Ashton reported a fall in sales revenue in the previous half-year, partly due to its decision to leave the De Beers run CSO and establish a direct marketing operation.
Robinson said in March that sales had picked up in early 1997 and predicted higher sales for the full year, but this week he told Reuters the company was feeling a squeeze on margins.
"If you use the comparable period, obviously we will be down (in the first half-year of 1997)," he said.
He said it was too early to predict annual profit, but Ashton hoped to top last year's net profit of A$20.57 million.
"We have not lost hope in doing that. It's too early in the year to forecast. I would not want, at this stage, to paint an optimistic or a pessimistic picture."
The full-year result would depend on how quickly the world market recovered from Russian selling, the strength of demand in key markets and exchange rate movements.
Russia has been exporting diamonds onto the open market, but its main diamond producer Almazy-Rossii-Sakha is expected soon to sign an agreement with the CSO to control Russian sales.
The London-based CSO controls about three-quarters of the world's US$4.5 billion-a-year trade in uncut diamonds. Russia typically accounts for about 20 percent of annual CSO sales.
"What we've seen is a market that's beginning to find indigestion with the amount of Russian material that came into the market during 1996 and the latter part of 1995," Robinson said.

"It will take a while before this Russian material washes through the system and I think once that happens then we'll will start to see some strengthening in prices and some change in the outlook," he added.
Despite the squeeze on profit margins, Ashton's share price has climbed over 15 percent since early this month, as reports emerge of exploration success in Canada.
Ashton's 62-percent owned subsidiary, Ashton Mining of Canada Inc, has so far reported finding diamonds in six of seven kimberlite pipes analysed so far in Alberta province.
Kimberlite is a type of rock associated with diamonds.
"I think we could say it's emerging as a new diamond province," Robinson said.
At 11.50 a.m. (0150 GMT) on Thursday, Ashton shares were one cent lower at A$2.25.
-- Mark Bendeich, Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
